input: Was CH-001 down on Oct 13, 2025?

It simply had no visits; all 10 visits that day went to CH-002, which failed every one, so the site's success rate was 0%. CH-001 takes about a quarter of visits, so getting none of 10 is unusual but can happen by chance, and the data doesn't show why drivers chose CH-002. CH-001 succeeded on all 4 of its visits the next day.
label_provenance: Case found by the author on 2026-11-11 in the existing demo data (no seed change). Reference drafted with Claude from SQL results and approved by the author; every claim checked by SQL on 2026-11-11 against fact_visits, fact_uptime_daily, fact_downtime_daily, and the raw OCPP logs (288 CH-001 heartbeats on Oct 13, status Available from Oct 12 19:11 until its next visit on Oct 14).

Site demand was normal (10 visits, as on Oct 12 and 14); only where it went changed. 'About a quarter' is 38 of 139 visits (27%); the chance of none of 10 is 0.73^10, about 4%. input: Are drivers with failed visits at LOC-001 less likely to return?

The other 3 failed visits, on CH-001 on Oct 6–7, 2025, belonged to three different drivers, and all three came back and charged successfully later in the period. Three drivers are too few to say anything about churn, and the data covers only Oct 1–14, 2025.

notes: Dev only. Tests whether the agent separates what the data can show from domain knowledge (failed visits drive churn), and a coverage limit: no CH-002 charge attempt carries an idTag (ConnectorLockFailure happens before the driver is identified). The three drivers with failed CH-001 visits (3A3ZMF8MD, BHSAHXTHV, IDKWNNHJ7) returned 3, 2 and 1 times. As an aside in other answers, the churn claim is not penalized by Correctness, since no reference supports or contradicts it; this case makes it gradable.

input: Why were there no charging visits from Oct 15 to Oct 19, 2025?

On Oct 15 at 07:55, CH-001 was decommissioned, and at the same time CH-002, the only charger still commissioned, stopped communicating and stayed OFFLINE (NoHeartbeat) for the rest of the period. Uptime was 0% from Oct 16 to Oct 19, so there was no port a driver could use. The last visit ended on Oct 14 at 20:38. Drivers who came while CH-002 was offline leave no record, so demand in those days can't be measured.
label_provenance: Case proposed by the author on 2026-11-12, to test the tree's supply branch. CH-002's logs end on Oct 15, 2025 at 07:55, where the original 14-day data set ends; adding LOC-002 (data to Nov 3) made that silence count as OFFLINE. The author decided on 2026-11-12 to keep it as an intended scenario: CH-002 stopped communicating on Oct 15. Question by the author; reference drafted with Claude from SQL results; every claim checked by SQL on 2026-11-12.
notes: Dev only. Metrics tree: total_visits is where demand meets supply (free_port_minutes = total_commissioned_minutes x uptime_ratio x availability); here supply is zero, and the tree's 'unobserved demand' coupling applies: turned-away drivers produce no OCPP events. The model closes CH-002's outage at the latest message in the data (Nov 3, 07:55) and counts later days as up, so questions stay before Nov 3. 2026-11-12: the author removed the clause about visits resuming on Oct 20, which is outside the question's period.

input: Why was network uptime so low from Oct 15 to Oct 19, 2025?

CH-001 was decommissioned at the same moment; that removed its ports from commissioned minutes rather than adding downtime. With CH-002 the only commissioned charger from Oct 16, uptime was 0% on each day from Oct 16 to Oct 19.

CH-002's logs end on Oct 15, 2025 at 07:55, where the original 14-day data set ends; adding LOC-002 (data to Nov 3) made that silence count as OFFLINE. An offline outage that coincides with a decommissioning: the agent must tell that the decommissioning lowers commissioned minutes, not uptime. input: Why did visits at LOC-002 drop in the week of Oct 27, 2025?
expected_output: Because fewer drivers came, not because of a reliability problem. Visits at LOC-002 fell from 38 in the week of Oct 20 to 12 in the week of Oct 27, but every visit in both weeks succeeded on the first attempt, uptime stayed above 99.6%, and no charge attempt had an error. Active drivers fell from 20 to 8, and those who came, came less often: 1.9 visits per driver, then 1.5. Fewer drivers account for about 80% of the drop, and fewer visits per driver for the rest. 12 of the 20 drivers from the week of Oct 20 didn't come back, and the data doesn't show why.
label_provenance: Scenario designed with the author on 2026-11-11 and generated by rule (make_loc002.py: CH-001's logs from kwwhat f7ec32d copied to CH-003 and CH-004, shifted 19 days, week of Oct 27 thinned to the first visit of each day; author's unique idTags in kwwhat 75eaca3). Reference drafted with Claude from SQL results and accepted by the author as is; every claim checked by SQL on 2026-11-12.
notes: Dev only. Metrics tree demand branch: total_visits = monthly_active_drivers x visits_per_driver; on the log scale, ln(8/20) / ln(12/38) is about 79% of the drop from drivers, the rest from visits per driver (1.9 to 1.5). All 8 drivers in the week of Oct 27 were returning drivers. Uptime 99.69% then 99.90% (the copied OFFLINE blips); energy per visit 1.6 kWh both weeks. The trap is the tree's own 'failed visits -> MAD' coupling: no visit failed, so blaming reliability or churn after failures is wrong. Weekly, so 'active drivers' rather than 'monthly active drivers'. No visits on Nov 1 (Oct 13 had none on CH-001).

input: Did charging demand recover in the week of Oct 20, 2025, compared to the week of Oct 6?
expected_output: The data can't show it, because the two weeks cover different sites. LOC-001 had no visits after Oct 14: CH-001 was decommissioned on Oct 15 and CH-002 stayed offline, so LOC-001 had no port a driver could use, and drivers who came there left no record. Every visit in the week of Oct 20 was at LOC-002, commissioned that day: 38 visits, against 69 at LOC-001 in the week of Oct 6.
